action_criteria.expected_evidence: Left posterior parietal 4.9 cm mass in the superior parietal lobule and precuneus with thick irregular ring enhancement, central necrosis, rim restricted diffusion, edema into the splenium and posterior limb, and 7 mm rightward midline shift; no infarct in an arterial distribution
action_criteria.label: Order MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol: DWI, FLAIR, post-contrast T1) to fully characterize the left posterior parietal lesion, define mass effect, and plan surgery
action_criteria.rationale: Contrast MRI with diffusion and FLAIR characterizes the lesion, separates it from an infarct, defines the mass effect and plans the surgical approach (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Maximum rCBV ratio 4.2 in the superior-anterior enhancing rim with an avascular necrotic core, supporting a high-grade neoplasm and targeting sampling
action_criteria.label: Order MR perfusion imaging (DSC perfusion) to assess tumor vascularity and identify the most vascular region to sample
action_criteria.rationale: Perfusion supports a high-grade neoplasm and identifies the most vascular region to sample; tissue decides the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Cho/NAA 13.7 with lipid-lactate in the enhancing component and raised choline at the superior perilesional margin
action_criteria.label: Order MR spectroscopy (1H-MRS) to characterize the tumor metabolic profile
action_criteria.rationale: Spectroscopy supports a high-grade neoplasm and shows infiltration beyond the enhancing margin; tissue decides the diagnosis.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No extracranial primary malignancy or visceral metastatic disease, supporting primary brain tumor as the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Order CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with contrast to exclude extracranial primary malignancy if solitary brain metastasis remains on the differential
action_criteria.rationale: A former smoker with a necrotic ring-enhancing mass: staging CT excludes an extracranial primary if a solitary metastasis is considered.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Glucose 143 mg/dL and HbA1c 7.4% in known type 2 diabetes, relevant to dexamethasone; electrolytes, platelets and coagulation normal: no laboratory contraindication to surgery
action_criteria.label: Order pre-operative laboratory workup: CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT), and type & screen in anticipation of surgical biopsy or resection
action_criteria.rationale: Surgery and corticosteroids are planned; coagulation, platelets, electrolytes, glucose and a group and screen are needed first.

action_criteria.label: Score performance status (Karnofsky and ECOG) at this visit
action_criteria.rationale: The choice between standard and hypofractionated chemoradiotherapy depends on age and Karnofsky performance status (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Left optic radiation compressed about 4 mm from the inferior enhancing margin; arcuate fasciculus about 7 mm and corticospinal tract about 12 mm from it
action_criteria.label: Order DTI tractography of the left optic radiation, arcuate fasciculus and corticospinal tract before resection
action_criteria.rationale: The tumor compresses the trigone, where the optic radiation runs (right inferior quadrantanopia), and its edema reaches the dominant parietal white matter and the posterior limb; tractography locates these tracts (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Integrated diagnosis Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4 with IDH1 R132H negative, ATRX retained, MGMT promoter methylated
action_criteria.label: Obtain tissue by maximal safe resection of the left posterior parietal lesion, or stereotactic biopsy if resection is not safely feasible, for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis with IDH1 R132H immunohistochemistry, ATRX immunohistochemistry and MGMT promoter methylation
action_criteria.rationale: Surgery is the first option for a resectable glioma and should be as extensive as safely possible (AIOM; EANO 2021). Only tissue establishes the integrated diagnosis and the molecular results that select treatment.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Steroid hyperglycemia on metformin, steroid plus aspirin GI risk and blunted losartan effect identified
action_criteria.label: Check drug interactions before initiating dexamethasone for vasogenic edema management, in the context of the patient's current medications (metformin, losartan, aspirin)
action_criteria.rationale: Dexamethasone worsens glycemic control on metformin, adds GI bleeding risk with aspirin and may raise blood pressure on losartan.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform lumbar puncture: the 7 mm midline shift creates a risk of herniation.
Do not initiate definitive tumor-directed therapy (radiation, temozolomide) before tissue diagnosis and molecular profiling are complete
Do not delay tissue diagnosis on the presumptive TIA diagnosis: a non-resolving focal deficit with an enhancing necrotic mass on MRI calls for a tumor work-up.
Do not start prophylactic antiseizure medication: the patient has had no seizure, and AIOM recommends against prophylaxis in brain tumour patients without a seizure history.
required_recommendations: Refer urgently to neurosurgery for maximal safe resection of the left posterior parietal lesion, with preoperative DTI tractography and intraoperative subcortical mapping, with stereotactic biopsy if resection is not safely feasible; send the specimen for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis (WHO CNS5).

Start dexamethasone for symptomatic vasogenic edema (for example 4 mg every 6 to 8 hours after a loading dose when mass effect is marked) at the lowest effective dose, with glucose monitoring and gastric protection, and taper after surgery.
Stop the aspirin started for presumed TIA: the deficit is explained by the tumor, and neurosurgery is planned.
Monitor capillary glucose at least every 6 hours on dexamethasone and adjust the antihyperglycemic regimen (metformin, adding insulin if needed), given type 2 diabetes with HbA1c 7.4%.

After the integrated diagnosis, refer to the neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team; for glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype at age 70 or under with KPS 70 or more, radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide (Stupp 2005; EANO 2021).

key_clinical_evidence: A progressive focal deficit over weeks (right hand clumsiness, right inferior quadrantanopia) with morning headache is not a TIA: it calls for urgent contrast-enhanced MRI

The MRI shows a left posterior parietal mass with thick irregular ring enhancement, central necrosis, rim restricted diffusion, edema into the posterior limb and 7 mm midline shift, and no arterial-territory infarct: a high-grade neoplasm on imaging
Perfusion (rCBV 4.2) and spectroscopy (Cho/NAA 13.7, lipid-lactate) support a high-grade neoplasm and target sampling; they do not grade the tumor
Only tissue gives the integrated diagnosis: IDH1 R132H negative at 60, ATRX retained, with microvascular proliferation and necrosis, is glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4; MGMT is methylated
7 mm midline shift makes lumbar puncture contraindicated
The tumor compresses the optic radiation at the trigone and approaches the dominant arcuate fasciculus, so DTI plans the resection; at 60 with KPS 80 the standard after surgery is the Stupp regimen
No seizure has occurred: antiseizure prophylaxis is not indicated (AIOM), and the aspirin started for presumed TIA is stopped

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Marcus Webb is a 60-year-old right-handed Black man with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia who presents to the neurology inpatient service after transfer from an outside urgent care, where he was initially evaluated for suspected transient ischemic attack. His wife reports that approximately five weeks ago he began complaining of a dull, persistent headache predominantly over the left parietal region, worse upon waking in the morning and accompanied by occasional mild nausea. He and his wife initially attributed this to stress and tension headaches related to the end-of-school-year administrative work. Over the past three weeks, his wife noticed that he was using his right hand less fluidly: he dropped a coffee cup, had difficulty buttoning his shirt, and struggled with his usual handwriting. When she expressed concern, he attributed the clumsiness to 'sleeping on his arm wrong.' Approximately ten days ago, a colleague noticed he seemed to have difficulty seeing things on his right side; he walked into a door frame on the right twice in one week. His primary care physician was contacted by phone and, in the context of his cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, prior smoking, age), provisionally attributed the right-sided symptoms to a possible transient ischemic attack and planned outpatient neuroimaging. He was given aspirin, counseled on stroke precautions, and told to follow up in one week. Two days later, the symptoms had not resolved and his wife brought him to an urgent care facility, where an expedited non-contrast head CT was performed showing a large hyperdense lesion in the left posterior parietal region with surrounding hypodensity and approximately 7 mm of rightward midline shift. He was transferred to the neurology service for further evaluation. He denies fever, chills, weight loss, known malignancy, recent head trauma, or prior neurological disease. He has no history of seizures.
